title: MATURITY IN MARRIAGE
mv: When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
mvp: “When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.’’ 1 Corinthians 13:11
assignment: Mention five (5) issues that can degenerate into a quarrel between a couple (2X5=10 marks).

b.x: Marriage is for adults who are mature, physically, financially, emotionally, relationally, spiritually, and in other key areas. Some people assume that age automatically equals maturity, but the two are different. Some individuals who are advanced in age still display childish behaviours, and these traits often strain their marriages. In this lesson, we shall explore the signs of immaturity and the essential qualities needed to build a strong marital relationship.
A. Comparison: These are couples who measure themselves against others. Paul points out in 2Corinthians 10:12 that those who engage in comparison lack understanding and wisdom.
B. Rivalry: This refers to unhealthy competition between spouses, which is contrary to the spirit of unity encouraged in Philippians 2:3-4.
C. The Blame Game: This is the failure or refusal of couples to take responsibility for their actions, but rather, shift blame and offer excuses for their shortcomings (Genesis 3:11-13).

D. Teleguiding: These are couples who always need external direction and cannot resolve issues without them degenerating into unresolved conflict. They still operate with a childish mindset, even though they are married (Matthew 18:15).
E. Unforgiveness: The inability to forgive easily, fault-finding and being unnecessarily petty, which births hatred and division in the marriage (Matthew 6:14-15).
F. Easily Provoked: This includes frequent outbursts of anger (Proverbs 15:18) and the use of rash and unfiltered words (James 1:19; Proverbs 29:11).
G. Selfishness: A self-centred or ego-driven attitude that prioritises personal needs over the spouse’s well-being (Philippians 2:4).
H. Malice: Displaying spiteful behaviour and refusing to make intentional efforts toward reconciliation (1 Peter 2:1; 1 Corinthians 14:20).

i: Willingness To Change: This is the readiness to change from negative to positive behaviour, acknowledge your faults, and make necessary corrections (1 Corinthians 6:7).
Mutual Respect: Grow to understand and value each other’s opinions, boundaries and emotions. Show mutual respect because respect is reciprocal (Romans 12:10; Ephesians 5:33).
Teachability: A marriage thrives when both partners are willing to learn, unlearn and relearn for the growth of their relationship.
Contentment: Being content, without slipping into complacency, promotes peace and strengthens the marital union (1 Timothy 6:6). This also includes being satisfied with one’s spouse (Proverbs 5:15).
Openness: Be expressive, rather than bottling issues, and keeping grudges. Avoid keeping secrets and walk in integrity (James 5:16; Ephesians 4:25; Job 31:6; Psalm 26:11).
Passion: Genuine affection helps couples to keep their focus on each other, while continually cherishing each other shows maturity.
Tolerance: Mature spouses learn to bear with each other’s weaknesses and accommodate their differences.
Apology And Gratitude: Humility is shown in offering sincere apologies and expressing appreciation, even for small acts of kindness.
Leave And Cleave: Cutting off unhealthy external influences and forming a strong marital bond is a sign of maturity (Genesis 2:24).
Finance: Financial stability reflects growth. Couples must seek financial knowledge, prioritise expenses, develop multiple streams of income, save, invest, and make prudent spending decisions.

Spiritual Growth: Abiding in Christ with evident fruits adds life to the marriage (John 15:5; Galatians 5:22-24). Couples should remain steadfast in faith, uphold God’s standard, and be passionate for Him.
Identify at least seven marks of maturity.
